content.thinking: Since there's no data to work with, I should write the postmortem honestly—root cause unknown, metrics unreadable, escalated for review—keeping impact stated as unbounded rather than inventing numbers, while flagging the assumption that the alert itself was genuine.

assumptions: The alert itself is assumed to be genuine; with no metrics retrieved, we cannot confirm that error rates were in fact elevated, nor rule it out.
The service is assumed to have remained in a faulty state after the escalation, because no recovery was observed before metrics collection ended - not because recovery was ruled out.

The reported error rate, outage duration, and customer impact are unknown. The elapsed time the automated responder held the incident (a fraction of a second) reflects how quickly it escalated, not how long the service was broken.
The empty feature-flag history is treated as 'no recent flag changes found', which is weak evidence at best given the metrics lookup failed in the same window; a flag-related cause is not excluded.
input.executive_summary:
An automated alert reported that one of our internal services was returning an elevated share of failed requests, starting on the morning of 28 September 2026. The automated responder picked the incident up immediately and tried to gather the service's own performance data, but no data came back, so it could not tell how many requests were failing, how many customers were affected, or why. It also checked whether any recent configuration change could explain the failures and found none. Within seconds the incident was handed to on-call engineers because there was not enough evidence to act on.

As of the last data available to this report, the service had not been seen to recover, so the disruption should be treated as ongoing and of unknown length. Customer impact is likewise unknown rather than zero: the absence of measurements is not evidence that nothing was affected. No remediation was applied by the automated responder; the only action taken was escalation to humans. The two gaps worth following up on are why the service's metrics could not be read during the incident, which blocked diagnosis entirely, and what the underlying fault actually was.
input.root_cause: Not established. The alert fired for an elevated error rate on io-shop, but the investigation retrieved zero minutes of metrics for the incident window and the feature-flag history showed no recent changes, so no candidate cause could be evaluated or ruled out; the incident was escalated to humans for insufficient evidence.
